teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A browser page and an API can be hosted at different addresses. Before blaming a rejected browser interaction on a bad login, separate two questions: are the addresses same-origin, and does the API permit this caller?

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: A browser origin is the combination of scheme, host and port; a difference in any of these makes two URLs cross-origin.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Browser same-origin restrictions limit a script's access to cross-origin responses unless the server permits that access through CORS. An API must check access at its endpoints independently of the browser's cross-origin restrictions.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Compare hypothetical URLs https://shop.example:443/orders and https://shop.example:443/items. Their paths differ, but their scheme, host and port match, so they share an origin. Changing the second host to api.example makes it cross-origin. Changing only the port to 8443 also makes it cross-origin. Browser permission to read the API response and endpoint permission to access the requested information remain separate checks. A browser access restriction is not a substitute for the latter.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Do not equate a browser-origin check with authentication. Even when browser access is permitted, the API must independently check access.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An orders service needs operations for reading an order, processing a new submission, replacing a known order and removing it. Choosing a method means choosing intended effects, not merely selecting a convenient label.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: A safe method has essentially read-only requested semantics; incidental effects such as logging do not make it unsafe.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: A method is idempotent when multiple identical requests have the same intended server effect as one request, even if responses differ. GET retrieves a selected representation and HEAD requests the same semantics without response content; both are safe and idempotent. POST requests resource-specific processing of submitted content and is not generally idempotent. PUT creates or replaces the target resource's state and DELETE removes its association with current functionality; both are idempotent but not safe.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: For the same order workflow, compare reading a representation with replacing one. A read asks what the current representation is; replacement asks the server to establish the submitted target state. Both can be idempotent, but only the first is safe because the replacement requests a change. Next compare replacement with collection-specific creation processing. Repeating the replacement still requests the same target state, whereas POST is not generally idempotent. This comparison gives a useful method-selection discipline: describe the intended effect in plain language before choosing the method. Then describe identical repetition separately. Do not decide idempotency from whether the first and second replies happen to look alike.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Picture an order at /orders/42. A GET retrieves its representation; HEAD asks for the same semantics without response content. Neither requests a change to the order. A log entry produced during retrieval is incidental, so it does not contradict safety. Now imagine sending the same replacement with PUT twice. The intended state after the second replacement is the same as after the first: that is idempotency, even though the returned responses may differ. DELETE similarly need not return identical responses on repetition to remain idempotent. In contrast, a POST asking the collection to process a new order is not generally idempotent. Work through each proposed operation with two separate questions: does it request a state change, and would identical repetition have the same intended effect? This separates safe retrieval from idempotent changes without treating them as the same property.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Safe does not mean absolutely no side effects, and idempotent does not mean identical responses. PUT and DELETE illustrate why an idempotent operation can still be unsafe.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A client sends an order as JSON and wants a JSON response. The outgoing body format, the response preference and the format actually returned are three different pieces of information.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Content-Type describes the media type of the associated representation, rather than the client's preferred response format.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Accept communicates acceptable response media types. For a JSON exchange, send Content-Type: application/json for JSON content and Accept: application/json to request a JSON response, and inspect the response Content-Type separately.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: For this exchange, Content-Type: application/json describes the submitted JSON content. Accept: application/json states the acceptable response media type. When examining the reply, inspect its own Content-Type rather than assuming the request header already established the response format. Think of Content-Type as a label attached to content and Accept as a preference sent by the client. Reading those labels separately makes it easier to describe what was sent and what came back.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Content-Type is not the client's preferred response format; Accept carries that preference.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Before writing a service function, describe the values it accepts and returns. A reader should be able to tell whether an order note can be missing as a value, and whether the caller may omit the argument altogether.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Annotate a function parameter with name: Type and its return value with -> Type; Python type hints alone do not enforce runtime validation.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Type | None permits None, while a default such as = None separately permits omitting a Python function argument. list[str], set[str], tuple[int, str] and dict[str, int] annotate a list of strings, a set of strings, a two-element integer/string tuple and a string-to-integer dictionary respectively.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: Read an interface in two passes. First read the shapes: which parameter is a string, which result is an integer, and which collection has a declared element or key/value type? Then read defaults: which arguments can be omitted? For the note example, removing = None changes omission behavior without removing None from the admitted type. Removing | None changes the admitted values without itself establishing a default. These small edits answer different questions. Type hints help express the intended interface, but a runtime value does not become validated merely because the function declaration describes it. A reader should be able to explain both passes before relying on the interface.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Consider a parameter written note: str | None. It admits a string or None, but without a default the caller must still supply an argument. Writing note: str | None = None adds permission to omit it. These are different decisions: the type describes permitted values, while the default describes what happens when the argument is not provided. For an order summary, list[str] can describe item names, set[str] can describe tags, tuple[int, str] can describe a two-part identifier/name value, and dict[str, int] can describe counts keyed by name. Read each annotation aloud rather than treating the brackets as decoration. The return annotation after -> describes the function result in the same way. None of these descriptions, by themselves, proves that actual runtime values have been checked. Keep the interface description separate from a future validation mechanism.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Adding a type hint does not add runtime validation. Also, allowing None is not the same as allowing an argument to be omitted.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Two order drafts need independent state. A class gives them a shared definition of behavior, but the two instances must not accidentally share a mutable collection intended to belong to just one draft.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: A class statement creates a class whose methods define behavior, and calling the class creates an instance.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Define __init__(self, ...) to initialize an instance and assign self.attribute to store that instance's state; an instance method receives that instance as its first argument. Instance variables hold data specific to each instance, while class variables are shared by instances of the class. A mutable class variable can be shared unintentionally; initialize a fresh mutable value on self inside __init__ when instances need independent values.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: Use the two drafts to test your understanding of ownership. Start with each draft intended to have an empty item collection. Change only the first draft and ask what state the second should have under the requirement of independence. If both are using one mutable class variable, that requirement is not met by merely calling the class twice. The corrective declaration is a fresh mutable value assigned on self inside initialization. Methods can be shared as class-defined behavior while their self argument identifies which instance is being operated on. This is the central separation: one definition of behavior can serve several instances whose state is meant to differ.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Imagine Draft is the class and draft_a and draft_b are two instances created by calling it twice. Its __init__ method assigns an item collection to self.items. Because initialization creates a fresh collection on each self, adding an item to draft_a belongs to that instance's state rather than to a shared class collection. Compare that with placing one mutable items value on the class: both instances can then see the shared value. Follow the ownership, not just the attribute name. The class defines the methods, and a method receives the particular instance as its first argument when operating on that instance. A useful reasoning exercise is to draw two instance boxes and write the intended state inside each. If both boxes point to one class-level collection despite requiring independence, the model does not match the requirement.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Having two instances does not make every attribute independent. A mutable class variable can still be shared; create fresh instance state inside __init__ when independence is required.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A service-related script reads a file, but the work inside that reading step might fail. The resource boundary should describe cleanup on both the successful path and the exceptional path.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Use with manager as resource: followed by an indented block to enter a managed resource scope.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: If __enter__ returns successfully, the with statement calls __exit__ when the block exits normally or through an exception. __exit__ receives exception details on exceptional exit and can suppress the exception by returning a true value; cleanup does not itself imply suppression. Using with open(...) as file closes the file after the block, including when an exception occurs.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: The boundary can be understood without designing a custom manager. Mark three points in the file example: successful entry, execution inside the block, and departure from the block. Departing normally and departing because of an exception both lead to file closure. For a general manager, a true __exit__ result can suppress an exception; that decision belongs to the manager and is separate from releasing the resource. Therefore a cleanup trace should not silently replace a failed operation with a successful one. State both outcomes explicitly: the resource exited its managed scope, and the exception was either propagated or intentionally suppressed under the manager behavior.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: In with open(...) as file, the indented block is the managed scope. Trace entry first: the manager enters successfully and supplies the resource used by the block. Trace normal exit next: leaving the block closes the file. Finally trace an exception raised while the block is using it: the managed exit still closes the file. That is the cleanup guarantee to rely on, conditional on successful entry. For a general manager, __exit__ also receives information about an exception and may suppress it by returning a true value. Therefore ask two questions separately: was the resource released, and was the failure propagated? Releasing a file does not itself mean that the failed work succeeded or that the exception was suppressed. Keep the useful work inside the indented resource boundary so that the scope is visible to the reader.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Cleanup and exception suppression are separate behaviors. Successful entry guarantees an exit call, not that exceptions disappear.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An asynchronous service task can contain several awaits without letting another task run at every one. To reason about concurrency, identify actual suspension rather than simply counting await keywords.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Calling an async def function produces a coroutine; awaiting it runs it and returns its result when it completes.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: An event loop uses cooperative scheduling, running one task at a time and allowing other tasks to run while a task waits on a pending future. An await can complete without suspension when its awaited operation completes immediately; the presence of await alone does not establish a switch to another task. When a future awaited by a suspended task completes, execution of that task's coroutine resumes. To trace suspension concretely, mark await asyncio.sleep(...) as a suspension point; sleep suspends the current task, including when its delay is zero.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: A useful execution sketch has two columns: current task and waiting condition. An immediately completed await leaves no pending wait to justify a handover. A suspended await has a pending future, so another runnable task may use the event loop while the first waits. When that future completes, the first task can resume. This sketch does not require claiming exactly which other task runs; it identifies the opportunity for cooperative scheduling. For asyncio.sleep, explicitly mark suspension even when the delay is zero. That exception to a casual "zero means immediate" intuition is why a careful trace uses documented operation behavior rather than guessing from the numeric argument.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Follow task A through an immediately completing coroutine and then through await asyncio.sleep(0). Calling the async function first creates a coroutine; awaiting it runs that coroutine and obtains its result. If that work completes immediately, A can continue without switching tasks. The sleep is different: even a zero delay suspends A, giving another runnable task an opportunity to execute. While A is suspended, the event loop still runs one task at a time; cooperative scheduling is not several tasks executing simultaneously in that loop. When the future A was waiting for completes, A resumes its coroutine. On paper, mark each operation as either completing immediately or waiting on a pending future, then mark only the latter as a possible handover, with sleep explicitly treated as suspension. This produces a more accurate execution trace than drawing an automatic switch after every await.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: An await is not proof that another task ran. Immediately completing awaited work can return without suspension; asyncio.sleep suspends even with delay zero.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: You want to add behavior around a service callable without rewriting the callable itself. A decorator lets another callable receive the function and determine what its name will refer to afterward.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: A decorator expression is evaluated when a function is defined, called with the function object, and its returned value is bound to the function name.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: @decorate above def function(...): applies decoration roughly like function = decorate(function). A callable wrapper can be built by defining an inner function that calls the supplied function and returning that inner function from the decorator.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Read @decorate above a function definition as roughly function = decorate(function). The decorator receives the function object, not the result of running that function with service data. A wrapper decorator can define an inner function that calls the supplied function and then return that inner function. The name now refers to what the decorator returned. Trace this in two stages: definition time applies the decorator and establishes the binding; a later call uses that bound value. If the returned value is the wrapper, the later call goes through the wrapper to the original callable. This distinction matters when reading service registration code: seeing @ above def means something happens while the function is defined, not just each time a request-related call is made. Keep the returned value in the trace rather than assuming decoration leaves the original binding untouched.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: A decorator is not merely a comment attached to a function. Its returned value becomes the binding for the function name.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Two backend projects may need different package versions. Installing everything into whichever interpreter happens to be on the machine makes it difficult to tell which project is using which dependencies.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: A virtual environment has a particular Python installation and its own installed packages, allowing applications to use different dependency versions.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Create an environment with python -m venv .venv and activate it with source .venv/bin/activate on Unix or .venv\Scripts\activate on Windows. Use python -m pip install package within the environment to install a dependency, and python -m pip show package to inspect its installed version and location. Check which python on Unix or where python on Windows to confirm that the interpreter path belongs to the activated environment.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: Separate the evidence in the environment exercise. The interpreter path tells you which Python command the shell resolves. Package inspection tells you the version and location visible through that interpreter. Together they make the dependency namespace concrete. If a teammate reports another installed version, first compare the two interpreter paths and package locations rather than assuming the project declaration changed. The environment is tied to a particular Python installation and has its own installed packages, so two applications can use different dependency versions. This explanation establishes environment isolation; recording declarations for reconstruction is a separate later task.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Create .venv for one project, activate it using the command for the operating system, and then inspect the interpreter path. On Unix, which python should point into that environment; on Windows, use where python. Only after identifying the interpreter should you install a dependency with python -m pip install package. Then inspect it with python -m pip show package, checking both version and location. The location is useful evidence that this project is using its own installed package rather than another environment's copy. Repeat the same reasoning for the second project: its environment has its own installed packages and a particular Python installation. Activation and installation are steps in establishing that boundary; the interpreter-path check confirms which boundary your current shell commands are actually using.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Do not treat an activation command alone as evidence that you inspected the right interpreter. Confirm the path, and inspect package version and location.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: When an HTTP request reaches a Python application, the network server and the application have different responsibilities. ASGI is the interface through which the server invokes the application and exchanges protocol events.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: An ASGI server handles the network connection and invokes an application callable through the ASGI interface.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: The application callable has the shape async def app(scope, receive, send), where scope describes the connection and receive and send exchange protocol events. Trace the application receiving http.request events through receive(), then sending http.response.start with status and headers followed by http.response.body through send().

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: Keep the scope and the event stream distinct in the drawing. Scope describes the connection passed to the application, whereas receive and send are used to exchange protocol events. For the response, status and headers belong to http.response.start, followed by body content through http.response.body. The order in that response trace matters: the metadata event and body event are not interchangeable names for a single application return. The network connection stays in the server box, and the ASGI callable stays in the application box. Understanding those roles is enough here; the learner does not need to implement connection handling to explain the request lifecycle.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Trace one request across the boundary. The server handles the network connection and invokes the async application callable. Its scope describes the connection; receive and send are the event-exchange callables supplied to it. The application receives http.request events through receive(). To produce its reply, it sends http.response.start containing status and headers, followed by http.response.body. Draw those events as arrows rather than treating the handler's return value as the entire network lifecycle. The start event and body event have different jobs: one establishes response metadata and the other carries body content. Keeping the server outside the application box also clarifies who owns the network connection and who participates in the ASGI protocol. You need to understand this event boundary without implementing a server from scratch.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: The application callable is not the component that directly owns all network handling. The ASGI server handles the connection and invokes the application through the interface.

teaching_blocks.content: An order needs a Python representation tied to a persistent database row. ORM mapping establishes that association, including which attribute identifies the row.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: A mapped class associates Python attributes with a database table's columns; first create the shared base with class Base(DeclarativeBase): pass, then inherit mapped entities from Base and declare attributes with Mapped[Type] and mapped_column(...).

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A browser wants to make a cross-origin call using a particular method and headers. For some requests it first asks whether that intended call is permitted, before sending the actual request.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: A browser preflights some cross-origin requests with OPTIONS to ask whether the intended method and headers are permitted before sending the actual request.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: A CORS preflight includes Origin and Access-Control-Request-Method; Access-Control-Request-Headers identifies requested headers when applicable. Verify a preflight by sending the caller's Origin and intended method and headers, then comparing Access-Control-Allow-Origin, Access-Control-Allow-Methods and Access-Control-Allow-Headers with that request. A credentialed cross-origin response requires an explicit allowed origin rather than * and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Trace an OPTIONS preflight for a hypothetical client origin https://shop.example that wants to use PUT with a content-type header. The preflight carries Origin and Access-Control-Request-Method, plus Access-Control-Request-Headers when requested headers need to be identified. Compare the reply's Access-Control-Allow-Origin, Access-Control-Allow-Methods and Access-Control-Allow-Headers with those requested values. This is a comparison between an intended call and the server's browser-access permission, not the actual operation's business response. If the cross-origin response is credentialed, look for an explicit allowed origin and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true rather than accepting a wildcard origin. teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An orders API needs clients to distinguish a successful creation, an absent order and an unexpected service failure. Status codes communicate those outcomes before the client interprets the body.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: HTTP status classes distinguish informational 1xx, successful 2xx, redirection 3xx, client error 4xx and server error 5xx outcomes.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Use 200 for a successful request, 201 when the request creates a resource, and 204 for successful completion with no response content. 400 denotes a perceived client request error, 401 lacks valid authentication credentials, 403 refuses fulfillment, 404 does not find or disclose the target, and 409 conflicts with current resource state. 500 denotes an unexpected server condition and 503 denotes temporary inability to handle the request, such as overload or maintenance.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: A useful review begins with the meaning of the outcome, not a memorized list of favorite codes. Ask whether the request succeeded, whether a client request problem prevents fulfillment, or whether an unexpected or temporary server condition prevents handling. Then distinguish cases within the class. Creation differs from retrieval; absent valid credentials differ from refusal; a conflict with current state differs from not finding or disclosing the target. These meanings let the same orders workflow produce intentionally different statuses. The response body can elaborate, but the status already conveys a defined outcome category. Do not use a successful status simply because a JSON body was produced.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Build an outcome table for a hypothetical order workflow. Successful retrieval can use 200; successful creation can use 201; successful completion with no response content can use 204. If the requested order is not found or disclosed, 404 fits that outcome. If a write conflicts with the current state, consider the declared 409 outcome. Keep credential problems separate from refusal: 401 means valid authentication credentials are lacking, whereas 403 denotes refusal to fulfill. Now compare unexpected failure with temporary inability to handle requests: those correspond to 500 and 503 respectively. First choose the outcome class, then the particular meaning within it. This avoids choosing every rejection as a generic 400 or every operational problem as the same server error. The table is about HTTP meaning, not a promise that a particular framework declaration will automatically produce each status.

teaching_blocks.content: Client errors and server errors convey different outcome classes. A no-content success is 204, not a promise of a response body.

teaching_blocks.content: Incoming order data needs a declared shape. Model validation turns compatible input into a model or explains why the input cannot satisfy that shape; it is not merely a test that the original values already had exact types.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters

Now inspect compatible conversion: the validated model can contain the declared type even though the original input did not already have it. The former illustrates conversion during validation; the latter raises ValidationError with field details. Compare those outcomes with omitting quantity entirely. All three cases answer different questions: was the field supplied, can its value satisfy the type, and what should omission produce when a default exists? Read the resulting model as validated output, not as proof that every input value started with the same type as the corresponding field.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An order rule should hold even when a database write comes from somewhere other than the API. Database constraints enforce row integrity at the stored-data boundary.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Declare a column as TYPE NOT NULL to reject nulls independently of whether a write came through an application.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Declare UNIQUE (columns) to reject duplicate combinations; PostgreSQL treats nulls as distinct by default unless NULLS NOT DISTINCT is specified. Declare PRIMARY KEY (columns) for unique non-null row identity; a primary key can contain more than one column. Declare FOREIGN KEY (columns) REFERENCES target (columns) so non-null referencing values must match referenced rows. Declare CHECK (condition) to constrain values in a row; a check passes when its expression is true or null, so use NOT NULL separately when absence must be rejected.

teaching_blocks.content: Consider hypothetical orders with an identity, a customer reference and a quantity. A PRIMARY KEY supplies unique non-null row identity and may use multiple columns. A FOREIGN KEY requires non-null references to match referenced rows. For a quantity that must be present and satisfy a row condition, combine NOT NULL with CHECK rather than asking CHECK alone to reject absence. A check expression that is null passes, so the two declarations cover different cases. For an external reference that should be unique, UNIQUE rejects duplicate combinations, but PostgreSQL treats nulls as distinct by default. If the requirement concerns null duplicates too, account for NULLS NOT DISTINCT. Work through one violating row at a time: null required value, duplicate identity, unmatched reference and failed condition. This identifies which constraint carries which rule instead of assuming application validation is the only place integrity lives.

teaching_blocks.content: CHECK does not replace NOT NULL: true or null passes a check. PostgreSQL UNIQUE also treats nulls as distinct by default.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A shared resource should be initialized before the service takes requests and released when request handling is finished. Its ownership belongs to the application lifetime, not to each individual handler.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: A lifespan context manages initialization before the application takes requests and cleanup after it finishes handling requests.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Define an @asynccontextmanager async function with acquisition before yield and cleanup after yield, and pass it as FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan). teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: Draw the lifespan as one long interval with several request intervals inside it. Acquisition precedes those request intervals; cleanup follows the period in which the application handles requests. Each handler uses the shared resource without repeating its startup work. This picture explains why the owner is lifespan even though requests are the consumers. If acquisition is instead repeated inside each handler, the ownership picture changes to per-request work and no longer illustrates the one-time startup goal. Keep the resource choice conditional on its intended application lifetime. The teaching point is explicit ownership around request handling, not that all resources should be global.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example

The application then serves requests using the acquired shared resource. Cleanup after yield belongs to shutdown after the application finishes handling requests. Pass that context to FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan). In a hypothetical service with a shared external client, draw one acquisition before the first request rather than one inside every handler invocation. Then draw one release after the request-handling lifetime. This makes the resource's ownership visible: requests use it, but lifespan owns its startup and cleanup. Sharing here avoids repeated startup work; do not treat the pattern as permission to share every kind of mutable object across requests.

teaching_blocks.content: Use Field(gt=..., ge=..., lt=..., le=..., multiple_of=...) to enforce exclusive bounds, inclusive bounds and divisibility on numeric values.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Two related order writes must succeed or fail together. A transaction makes that joint boundary explicit rather than letting each write be treated as independently durable.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Use async with session.begin(): around related writes to commit on successful exit and roll back on exceptional exit.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: A commit makes transaction changes durable, while a rollback discards uncommitted changes; multiple related writes belong in one transaction when they must succeed or fail together. After a flush failure, explicitly roll back before reusing that session; a failed flush leaves its transactional state requiring recovery.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: Transaction recovery is observable separately from the original failure. In the two-write example, successful completion of the pair belongs to commit; exceptional exit belongs to rollback. A failed flush requires explicit rollback before session reuse even when application code has already caught the error. Therefore the recovery path should mention both the discarded uncommitted changes and the session state that must be recovered. Reporting only that an error was handled obscures whether either responsibility was met. Group the writes because the requirement ties their success together, and keep that requirement visible in the transaction scope.

teaching_blocks.content: Place related writes inside async with session.begin(). Successful exit commits; exceptional exit rolls back. The grouping should come from the requirement that the writes succeed or fail together, not merely from their proximity in the source file.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Repeated reads of an order may reuse a cached copy, but the database remains authoritative. Cache-aside separates accelerated reads from source-of-truth storage.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Cache-aside keeps a cache in front of a primary store; the primary store remains the source of truth rather than the cache becoming authoritative storage.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: On a read, get the cache key first; on a miss, load from the primary store, cache the result and return it to the caller. Compare a hit and a miss in a two-path diagram, keeping both connected to the same represented result. The cache is a disposable copy; the primary store is still the authority when deciding what the stored order actually is.

teaching_blocks.content: A cache hit does not make the cache authoritative. A key must distinguish results whose identity or parameters differ.
